procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 22, 1966 of the Punjab High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 26 of 1966 and Murder Reference No. 2 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge convicted accused 1 and 5 of offences under sections 302 and 201 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced them to death and five years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court altered the convictions to those under sections 302 and 201 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and confirmed the sentences.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Accused 1 and 5, the two appellants, filed an appeal by special leave to the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants could be altered from an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code to one under Section 302 read with Section 34, and whether such an alteration caused any prejudice to them.

facts: The appellants were initially convicted by the Sessions Judge under Section 302 (murder) read with Section 149 (unlawful assembly) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
On appeal, the High Court altered the conviction to Section 302 read with Section 34 (common intention) of the IPC.
The appellants challenged this alteration in the Supreme Court, arguing it was improper and caused them prejudice.
law: A court can alter a conviction from an offence under Section 302/149 IPC to one under Section 302/34 IPC if the evidence on record supports the ingredients of the latter offence.
application: The Supreme Court examined the evidence ("materials on the record") and found that it clearly showed that the murder was committed by six culprits, including the two appellants.
The Court determined that this act was done "in furtherance of the common intention of all" the participants.
Since the evidence established a common intention to commit murder, the requirements for a conviction under Section 34 were met.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument, holding that the conviction could be altered from Section 302/149 to Section 302/34. It concluded that because the evidence on record clearly established that the murder was committed in furtherance of a common intention shared by all culprits, the alteration caused no prejudice to the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants could be altered from an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code to one under Section 302 read with Section 34, and whether such an alteration caused any prejudice to them.
appellant_arguments: When a specific group of named individuals are charged with murder under a common intention (Section 34), and a majority of them are acquitted, the remaining accused cannot be convicted under the same provision.
Since four of the six named co-accused were acquitted, it is legally impossible to convict the remaining two for acting in furtherance of a common intention with the acquitted persons.
As it is not known who delivered the fatal blow, the appellants cannot be convicted under Section 302 individually, and without a finding of common intention with others, they must be acquitted.
respondent_arguments: The acquittal of some named accused does not mean that the convicted appellants acted alone. It only means the prosecution failed to prove the identity of those specific co-accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
The court can still find that the appellants shared a common intention to commit murder with other, unidentified assailants.

As long as the evidence establishes that the appellants participated in the crime along with others (even if unidentified) in furtherance of a common intention, a conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 is valid.

cases.principle: The principle which section 34 embodies is the participation in some action with the intention of committing a crime; once such participation is established, s. 34 is at once attracted.
The principle which section 34 embodies is the participation in some action with the intention of committing a crime; once such participation is established, s. 34 is at once attracted.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where multiple named accused are charged with an offense read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, the acquittal of some of the accused does not prevent the conviction of the remaining accused under the same provision. Once it is established that a criminal act was committed in furtherance of the common intention of all participants, each participant is liable for the act as if it were done by them alone, even if the specific part played by each individual is unknown.
obiter: Section 34 is intended to meet a case where members of a party acted in furtherance of the common intention of all but it was difficult to prove exactly the part played by each of them.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a group of named accused are charged with murder under Section 34 and some are acquitted, the remaining accused can still be convicted under the same section if the court, on a proper appraisal of the evidence, finds that the convicted individuals participated in the crime with other, unidentified assailants. The acquittal of named persons only signifies a failure to prove their specific identity, not that other participants did not exist. As long as the evidence shows the convicted persons acted in furtherance of a common intention with a group, they are liable for the murder as if they had committed it alone.
legal_tests_applied: To attract Section 34, the prosecution must establish participation in some action with the intention of committing a crime.

Where some named co-accused are acquitted, the remaining accused can be convicted under Section 34 if the court can find from the evidence that other unidentified assailants, together with the convicted accused, took part in the crime in furtherance of the common intention of all.
why_appellant_lost: The acquittal of the four named co-accused did not mean they could not have participated in the murder; it only meant their identity was not proven. The court found that the witnesses were simply mistaken as to the identity of the other four culprits.
The materials on record clearly showed that the murder was committed by six culprits, including the two appellants, in furtherance of the common intention of all.
The alteration of the charge from an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 to one under Section 302 read with Section 34 caused no prejudice to the appellants.
why_respondent_won: Once it was found that the murders were committed in furtherance of the common intention of all participants, each person was liable as though the murders had been committed by him alone, even if it was not known which particular person gave the fatal blows.
The court found that the two appellants participated in the offence with four other culprits, even if those four were unidentified, satisfying the requirement for common intention under Section 34.
The principle of Section 34 is participation with a criminal intention; once the appellants' participation with others was established, the section was immediately attracted.
policy_considerations: Section 34 is intended to meet a case where members of a party acted in furtherance of the common intention of all but it was difficult to prove exactly the part played by each of them.
